distractors.B: The problem is not latency; even if sentiment ran instantly, it would still be routing on the wrong signal.
distractors.C: Training feasibility is not the issue; sentiment can be detected but is simply the wrong criterion for an escalation decision.
distractors.D: Explicit requests for a human are recognized from what the customer states, not inferred from sentiment; this option misstates how explicit-request escalation works.

scenario: To decide escalation, an engineer wants the agent to output a numeric self-assessed confidence for each case and hand off to a human whenever the value is below 7 out of 10.
stem: What is the primary weakness of this confidence-threshold approach?

options.text: A 7-out-of-10 cutoff is too high and should be lowered to 5 so fewer cases escalate.
LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so the agent is often confidently wrong on hard cases and needlessly uncertain on easy ones, misrouting exactly where it matters.
Confidence scores add too many tokens to each response, raising cost beyond acceptable limits.
Confidence scores work well but must be averaged over at least ten turns before they can be trusted.

rationale.correct: Self-reported confidence is an unreliable proxy for complexity because model confidence is poorly calibrated: the agent tends to be confidently wrong on precisely the difficult cases that should escalate, so thresholding on it reinforces the miscalibration instead of correcting it.

distractors.A: Tuning the threshold does not fix an uncalibrated signal; whether the cutoff is 5 or 7, the underlying score does not reliably track actual difficulty.
distractors.C: Token cost is negligible and is not the reason the approach fails; the failure is that the signal itself is untrustworthy.
distractors.D: Averaging an uncalibrated score over more turns does not make it calibrated; the defect is in what the score measures, not in the sample size.

scenario: A customer is clearly annoyed and writes that shipping took too long, but the request is a standard reshipment the agent is fully authorized to process. The customer has not asked for a human.
stem: What is the best-calibrated response?

options.text: Escalate immediately, because the customer's evident frustration signals the case is beyond the agent's scope.
Ignore the emotional tone and process the reshipment silently without acknowledging the customer's experience.
Acknowledge the frustration and offer to resolve the reshipment now, since it is within the agent's capability, escalating only if the customer reiterates a preference for a human.
Ask the customer to rate their frustration numerically, then decide whether to escalate based on the rating.

rationale.correct: When the issue is within the agent's capability, the right pattern is to acknowledge the frustration while offering to resolve it, and to escalate only if the customer reiterates a preference for a human. Frustration alone is not an escalation trigger.

distractors.A: Frustration is not a reliable proxy for complexity or scope; escalating a routine reshipment the agent can handle wastes a human touch and lowers first-contact resolution.
distractors.B: Processing silently ignores the customer's stated experience; good practice acknowledges frustration even while resolving, which improves the interaction without requiring escalation.
distractors.D: A self-rated frustration score is an unreliable basis for the decision and adds friction; the case should simply be resolved unless the customer asks for a human.

scenario: An agent handling an account-access issue has exhausted its available tools and retries: the identity check keeps failing on a corrupted record, and it has cycled several times without advancing toward a resolution.
stem: Which escalation trigger does this situation represent, and what should the agent do?

options.text: No trigger applies yet; the agent should keep retrying the same identity check until it eventually succeeds.
A sentiment trigger; the agent should escalate only once the looping causes the customer to become frustrated.
A confidence trigger; the agent should lower its confidence threshold so this case falls under it.
An inability-to-make-meaningful-progress trigger; the agent should escalate to a human with a structured handoff rather than loop indefinitely.

rationale.correct: Inability to make meaningful progress is an explicit escalation trigger. Once the agent has genuinely stalled with no path forward, it should escalate to a human rather than loop, ideally providing a structured handoff so the human can continue.

distractors.A: Retrying a check that keeps failing is the anti-pattern the trigger exists to prevent; endless looping neither resolves the case nor respects the customer's time.
distractors.B: Tying escalation to whether the customer becomes upset routes on sentiment, an unreliable proxy; the case warrants escalation on its own because progress has stalled, regardless of tone.
distractors.C: Adjusting a self-reported confidence threshold relies on a miscalibrated signal; the concrete, observable fact that no progress is being made is the sound basis for escalating.

scenario: A hub-and-spoke research system has a web search subagent that times out while researching a complex subtopic. You are designing how this failure flows back to the coordinator.
stem: Which error propagation approach best enables the coordinator to make an intelligent recovery decision?

options.text: Return structured error context to the coordinator including the failure type, the attempted query, any partial results, and potential alternative approaches.
Retry inside the subagent with exponential backoff and, once retries are exhausted, return a generic "search unavailable" status.
Catch the timeout inside the subagent and return an empty result set marked as successful.
Propagate the timeout exception to a top-level handler that terminates the entire research workflow.

rationale.correct: Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternative approaches) gives the coordinator what it needs to decide whether to retry with a modified query, try an alternative source, or proceed with partial results and annotate the gap.

distractors.B: Local retry is reasonable for transient failures, but collapsing the outcome into a generic "search unavailable" status hides the attempted query and partial results, so the coordinator cannot make an informed recovery decision.
distractors.C: Marking a failure as an empty successful result silently suppresses the error, prevents any recovery, and risks shipping an incomplete report that looks complete.
distractors.D: Terminating the whole workflow on one subagent failure is disproportionate; other subagents succeeded and recovery strategies could still produce a usable result.

scenario: A subagent queries an internal knowledge base for documents about a product feature. The query executes successfully and returns zero matching documents.
stem: How should the subagent report this outcome so the coordinator responds appropriately?

options.text: Report it as a retryable access failure so the coordinator schedules another attempt against the same knowledge base.
Report it as a valid empty result: the query succeeded and simply had no matches, so no retry is warranted.
Report a generic "knowledge base unavailable" status so the coordinator treats it as a service outage.
Raise a fatal error that halts the workflow because the requested documents could not be found.

rationale.correct: A successful query that returns no matches is a valid empty result, distinct from an access failure. Reporting it accurately tells the coordinator the source has nothing on this topic, so it should annotate coverage or try a different source rather than retry.

distractors.A: An access failure implies the query could not complete and may succeed on retry. Here the query completed fine, so retrying wastes effort and misleads the coordinator about what happened.
distractors.C: A generic unavailability status conflates a working source that has no matches with a broken one, hiding the real signal and prompting inappropriate retries.
distractors.D: A valid empty result is expected data, not a fatal condition; halting the workflow over it is a terminate-all anti-pattern.

scenario: A subagent experiences an intermittent connection reset on its first API call to an external search service. A single immediate retry succeeds and returns full results.
stem: What is the correct error-propagation behavior for this subagent?

options.text: Immediately propagate the first connection reset to the coordinator without attempting recovery.
Handle the transient failure locally with the retry, then return the successful results and do not propagate the resolved error.
Return the results but also flag the task as failed because an error occurred at any point during execution.
Suppress the results and report an empty successful set to keep the coordinator's logic simple.

rationale.correct: Subagents should perform local recovery for transient failures and only propagate errors they cannot resolve. A resolved transient failure needs no propagation; the subagent returns the successful results.

distractors.A: Propagating every transient blip pushes recoverable noise up to the coordinator, defeating the purpose of local recovery and causing unnecessary coordinator-level handling.
distractors.C: The task actually succeeded after recovery. Flagging it as failed misreports the outcome and could trigger needless re-delegation.
distractors.D: Discarding good results and reporting an empty success is the suppress-as-success anti-pattern; it throws away work the subagent completed.

scenario: One of five parallel research subagents fails permanently: its data source is down and local retries did not help. The other four returned strong findings. The synthesis agent must now produce a report.
stem: How should the synthesis output handle the missing subagent's topic area?

options.text: Omit any mention of the failure and present the four successful areas as if they were the complete scope.
Discard the entire report because one topic area could not be researched.
Include coverage annotations indicating which findings are well-supported and flagging the topic area that has a gap due to an unavailable source.
Fill the gap by having the synthesis agent infer plausible findings for the missing topic from general knowledge.

rationale.correct: Synthesis output should carry coverage annotations: mark which findings are well-supported and explicitly flag the topic area that is incomplete because a source was unavailable. This preserves honesty about scope and lets the reader judge completeness.

distractors.A: Presenting partial coverage as complete silently suppresses the gap, the same class of error as marking a failure as success.
distractors.B: Discarding four solid areas because one failed is the terminate-all anti-pattern; partial results still have value when the gap is disclosed.
distractors.D: Fabricating findings from general knowledge to paper over a real gap produces unsupported claims and undermines provenance.

scenario: During review you find every subagent in a system wraps all failures in a single string status, "data retrieval error," before returning to the coordinator. The coordinator's recovery logic rarely does anything useful.
stem: Why does this generic status undermine coordinator recovery?

options.text: It is too verbose for the coordinator to parse, so the coordinator times out reading it.
It hides the failure type, attempted query, and partial results, leaving the coordinator no basis to choose retry, an alternative approach, or proceeding with partial data.
It causes the coordinator to always retry, which is the ideal behavior for every failure.
It violates the API contract because status fields must always be numeric error codes.

rationale.correct: A generic status strips the context the coordinator needs. Without the failure type, the attempted query, and any partial results, the coordinator cannot distinguish a retryable timeout from a valid empty result or a permission error, so it cannot pick an appropriate recovery.

distractors.A: The problem is too little information, not too much; a short generic string is trivial to parse but useless for decisions.
distractors.C: Blindly retrying every failure is itself harmful, for example retrying a valid empty result or a permanent permission error wastes effort and never succeeds.
distractors.D: There is no rule requiring numeric-only status codes; structured error context is deliberately richer than a single code.

scenario: A team is debating how a subagent should surface a hard failure. One engineer proposes returning an empty result flagged as success "so the pipeline never breaks," and another proposes throwing an exception that tears down the whole multi-agent run.
stem: What is the best characterization of these two proposals?

options.text: Both are sound; choose whichever is simpler to implement.
The empty-as-success approach is correct, and terminating the workflow is the only real anti-pattern.
Terminating the workflow is correct, and empty-as-success is the only real anti-pattern.
Both are anti-patterns: empty-as-success silently suppresses the error, and terminating the whole workflow overreacts to a single failure; the subagent should instead return structured error context.

rationale.correct: Silently suppressing errors (empty results as success) and terminating the entire workflow on a single failure are both named anti-patterns. The right move is structured error context so the coordinator can recover proportionately.

distractors.A: Neither is sound; both destroy the coordinator's ability to recover intelligently, so implementation ease is irrelevant.
distractors.B: Empty-as-success is itself an anti-pattern because it masks failure as valid data, so it is not the correct approach.
distractors.C: Terminating the workflow overreacts to one recoverable failure, so it is not correct either.

scenario: A subagent's structured error report reaches the coordinator: failure_type is "timeout", attempted_query captured, partial_results contain two of an expected six sources, and alternative_approaches suggests a narrower query or a secondary index.
stem: Which coordinator behavior best uses this structured context?

options.text: Evaluate the context and choose a recovery: retry with the narrower query or secondary index, keep the two partial sources, and annotate the synthesis if the gap persists.
Ignore the partial results and re-run the identical query unchanged until it eventually succeeds.
Treat the timeout as a valid empty result and record that the topic has no relevant sources.
Abort the run and return the error to the user, since a timeout means the research cannot be completed.

rationale.correct: The whole point of structured context is to enable an informed choice: the coordinator can retry using a suggested alternative, retain the partial results already gathered, and disclose any remaining gap in the synthesis. That is intelligent, proportionate recovery.

distractors.B: Re-running the exact query that just timed out ignores the alternative approaches and discards the partial results, so it is likely to fail the same way.
distractors.C: A timeout is an access failure, not a valid empty result; recording "no relevant sources" misrepresents the situation and suppresses a recoverable gap.
distractors.D: Aborting throws away four other subagents' work and the partial results; a single timeout does not justify terminating the workflow.

scenario: You are defining the return contract for subagents in a multi-agent system so the coordinator can always reason about outcomes, whether a query succeeded, returned nothing, or failed.
stem: Which contract best supports intelligent coordinator recovery across all these cases?

options.text: A single boolean success flag plus a free-text message, leaving the coordinator to infer the rest.
Only the result payload on success and an uncaught exception on any failure, with no distinction between failure kinds.
A structured result that distinguishes valid empty results from access failures and, on failure, includes failure type, attempted query, partial results, and alternative approaches.
A normalized generic status string for every non-ideal outcome so the coordinator has one uniform code path.

rationale.correct: A contract that separates valid empty results from access failures and, on failure, carries failure type, attempted query, partial results, and alternatives gives the coordinator everything it needs to retry, reroute, or proceed with an annotated gap.

distractors.A: A boolean plus free text forces the coordinator to parse prose and cannot reliably separate an empty result from a timeout, so recovery decisions become guesswork.
distractors.B: Raising uncaught exceptions with no failure taxonomy tends toward terminating the workflow and erases partial results and the empty-versus-failure distinction.
distractors.D: Collapsing every outcome into one generic status is the exact anti-pattern that hides valuable context, even though it looks uniform.

scenario: An agent has spent two hours exploring a large Java monorepo. Early on it correctly named the specific classes (`RefundProcessor`, `LedgerClient`) involved in the refund flow. Now, late in the session, when asked a follow-up it answers vaguely that 'a typical service usually delegates to a payment handler,' and its answers to the same question differ between attempts.
stem: What does this behavior most directly indicate?

options.text: Context degradation in the extended session: as the context window fills, the model loses grip on specifics it discovered earlier and falls back on generic 'typical pattern' reasoning and inconsistent answers.
The underlying model was silently downgraded to a smaller variant partway through the session, reducing its reasoning capacity.
The codebase changed on disk during the session, so the classes the agent found earlier no longer exist.
The agent's temperature setting is too high, which is the root cause of both the vagueness and the inconsistency.

rationale.correct: These are the textbook symptoms of context degradation in an extended session: the model starts giving inconsistent answers and references 'typical patterns' instead of the specific classes it discovered earlier, because the concrete findings have been pushed out of or diluted within the context window.

distractors.B: There is no model swap; the guide attributes this pattern to context filling up over a long session, not to a hidden capacity change.
distractors.C: Nothing indicates the source changed on disk; the specifics were verified earlier and the regression is in the agent's recall, not the code.
distractors.D: Temperature affects sampling randomness generally but is not what the guide identifies as the cause of losing earlier-discovered specifics in a long exploration; the diagnosis is context degradation.

scenario: You are guiding an agent through a multi-day exploration of an unfamiliar codebase. You want later questions to still benefit from specific facts (exact class names, file paths, call chains) discovered early, even after the context window has turned over many times.
stem: Which practice most directly counteracts context degradation across these boundaries?

options.text: Raise the max_tokens on every request so responses can restate everything discovered so far.
Have the agent maintain a scratchpad file that records key findings, and reference that file when answering subsequent questions.
Instruct the agent to never end its turn so the single conversation never loses its history.
Lower the difficulty of questions asked after the first hour so the model does not need the earlier specifics.

rationale.correct: Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries. By writing discoveries to a file and re-reading them for later questions, the agent recovers specific facts that would otherwise be lost as context degrades, without depending on them staying resident in the window.

distractors.A: Larger max_tokens governs output length, not retention of prior findings; it does nothing to stop earlier specifics from being pushed out of context.
distractors.C: Keeping one turn open indefinitely still accumulates and eventually overruns the same context window, so degradation still occurs; it does not externalize the findings.
distractors.D: Avoiding hard questions sidesteps the task rather than preserving the discovered information; the goal is to retain specifics, not to stop needing them.

scenario: The main agent must build and hold a high-level understanding of a system's architecture. Answering the architecture questions requires several noisy sub-investigations, such as 'find all test files' and 'trace every dependency of the refund flow,' each of which produces pages of verbose output.
stem: How should the work be structured to protect the main agent's context?

options.text: Run every sub-investigation inline in the main agent so all raw output stays visible for maximum fidelity.
Delegate each verbose sub-investigation to a subagent that returns only a concise result, while the main agent coordinates the high-level understanding.
Skip the sub-investigations and have the main agent guess the architecture from file names alone.
Paste the full output of each sub-investigation into a system prompt so it is cached and cannot be evicted.

rationale.correct: Subagent delegation isolates verbose exploration output in the subagent's own context. The subagent absorbs the noise and returns a distilled answer, so the main agent's window stays focused on coordinating high-level understanding.

distractors.A: Running everything inline floods the main agent's context with verbose discovery output, which is exactly what accelerates context degradation.
distractors.C: Guessing abandons the investigation entirely and produces the vague 'typical pattern' answers the approach is meant to prevent.
distractors.D: Stuffing full raw output into the system prompt still consumes the context budget (and bloats every request); the point of delegation is to keep that verbosity out of the main agent.

scenario: A long-running multi-agent exploration crashes midway. On resume, you do not want to redo hours of investigation. Your design has each subagent export its state to a known location, and the coordinator reloads on restart.
stem: What is the coordinator's role in this crash-recovery design?

options.text: Load a manifest of the exported agent states on resume and inject the recovered state into the agents' prompts so work continues from where it stopped.
Re-spawn every subagent from scratch with empty context, since exported state cannot be trusted after a crash.
Replay the entire original conversation transcript token-for-token to rebuild the exact prior context.
Increase the number of subagents on resume so the extra parallelism compensates for the lost progress.

rationale.correct: Structured state persistence for crash recovery works by each agent exporting state to a known location; on resume the coordinator loads a manifest of those exports and injects the recovered state into agent prompts, so the session continues rather than restarting.

distractors.B: Re-spawning with empty context discards the very state the design exported to enable recovery, defeating its purpose.
distractors.C: Replaying the full transcript is not the mechanism and would re-consume enormous context; recovery is driven by the compact exported state manifest, not the raw history.
distractors.D: Adding subagents does not recover lost findings; it just redoes work without loading the persisted state.

scenario: During an extended exploration, the main agent's context has filled with verbose discovery output (long file listings, full grep results, tool transcripts). The essential conclusions are already captured, but the window is nearly saturated and responses are slowing and drifting.
stem: Which action most directly reduces context usage so the session can continue effectively?

options.text: Start a brand-new, unrelated conversation and hope the model remembers the prior findings.
Use `/compact` to condense the accumulated context, shrinking the verbose discovery output while retaining the essentials.
Delete the scratchpad files to free disk space so the model has more room to think.
Lower the model's temperature to zero to make the remaining context take up less space.

rationale.correct: `/compact` is the tool for reducing context usage during extended exploration when the window fills with verbose discovery output; it condenses the accumulated context while preserving what matters so work can continue.

distractors.A: A fresh unrelated conversation carries none of the prior findings forward and relies on false memory, losing the work instead of compacting it.
distractors.C: Scratchpad files live on disk, not in the context window; deleting them destroys persisted findings and does nothing to reduce context usage.
distractors.D: Temperature controls sampling randomness and has no effect on how many tokens the accumulated context occupies.

scenario: An exploration is organized into phases. Phase 1 mapped the data model; Phase 2 will trace the request lifecycle and will spawn several subagents. You want Phase 2's subagents to start already aware of Phase 1's conclusions without inheriting all of Phase 1's raw output.
stem: What is the recommended way to carry Phase 1's knowledge into Phase 2?

options.text: Summarize Phase 1's key findings and inject that summary into the initial context of the Phase 2 subagents.
Give each Phase 2 subagent the full raw transcript of Phase 1 so nothing is lost.
Rely on the subagents to independently rediscover Phase 1's findings, since they share the coordinator's memory.
Delay all summarization until the very end so no intermediate detail is prematurely discarded.

rationale.correct: The guide's skill is to summarize key findings from one exploration phase before spawning subagents for the next, injecting those summaries into the new agents' initial context. This transfers understanding compactly without the verbose raw output.

distractors.B: Injecting the full raw transcript reintroduces the verbose output the phased/summary approach exists to avoid, quickly saturating the new subagents' context.
distractors.C: Subagents run with isolated context and do not share the coordinator's memory, so relying on rediscovery both wastes effort and risks inconsistency.
distractors.D: Deferring all summarization defeats the purpose of injecting phase summaries up front; the next phase needs the condensed findings at its start.

scenario: A teammate proposes handling every long exploration purely by calling `/compact` repeatedly whenever the window gets full, with no scratchpad files and no subagents. They argue compaction alone solves context management.
stem: What is the strongest limitation of a compact-only strategy?

options.text: `/compact` permanently corrupts tool-use history, so agents can no longer call tools afterward.

Compaction reduces in-context volume but is lossy and stays inside one agent's window; it does not durably persist specific findings to a known location or isolate verbose exploration the way scratchpad files and subagent delegation do.
`/compact` can only be run once per session, so it cannot help a session that fills repeatedly.
Compaction increases context usage rather than reducing it, so it makes degradation worse.

rationale.correct: Compaction is one tool among several. It condenses context in place but is lossy and offers no durable, out-of-context store or crash recovery; scratchpad files persist specifics to a known location and subagent delegation isolates verbose output. A robust strategy combines them.

distractors.A: There is no such corruption; compaction condenses context, it does not disable tool use.
distractors.C: `/compact` can be used repeatedly during a session as verbose output accumulates; a single-use limit is fabricated.
distractors.D: Compaction reduces context usage; claiming it increases usage inverts its purpose.

scenario: You are designing crash recovery for a fleet of exploration subagents. A colleague suggests the coordinator keep all subagent findings only in its own live conversation history and reconstruct everything from that history if a crash occurs.
stem: Why is a structured state export with a coordinator-loaded manifest preferable to relying on the coordinator's live history?

options.text: Live conversation history is lost when the process crashes and is subject to context degradation while running; exporting each agent's state to a known location gives a durable manifest the coordinator can reload and inject on resume.
The coordinator's live history is automatically written to disk by the API after every turn, so a manifest would be redundant.
Manifests are only useful for billing reconciliation and have no role in resuming interrupted work.
A manifest must contain the full verbose output of every subagent, which is why it survives crashes better than history.

rationale.correct: Live history is volatile: a crash loses it, and even while running it degrades as context fills. Exporting each agent's state to a known location produces a durable manifest the coordinator loads on resume and injects into agent prompts, which is exactly the crash-recovery design the guide describes.

distractors.B: The API does not persist your conversation history to disk for you; assuming automatic durable storage is a dangerous misconception that leaves work unrecoverable.
distractors.C: The manifest's purpose here is resuming interrupted exploration by reloading exported state, not billing.
distractors.D: The manifest holds structured, compact state, not full verbose output; loading everything raw would resaturate context and undermine the design.

scenario: Your invoice-extraction agent reports 97% overall accuracy across a 10,000-document evaluation set, and leadership wants to switch off human review entirely to cut costs. The set is dominated by clean single-page domestic invoices; scanned multi-page international invoices make up only 4% of the volume.
stem: Why is the 97% aggregate figure an unsafe basis for eliminating human review?

options.text: A single aggregate number can mask systematically poor performance on low-volume segments like scanned international invoices, whose errors are diluted by the large clean-invoice majority.
Accuracy above 95% is statistically meaningless because the confidence interval is always too wide to act on.
Aggregate accuracy is only valid if it is recomputed after every single extraction in production.
The number is unsafe purely because 10,000 documents is far too small a sample to estimate any accuracy at all.

rationale.correct: An aggregate metric is a volume-weighted average, so a segment that is only 4% of the data can be extracted almost entirely wrong while the overall number stays near 97%. You cannot automate safely until you know accuracy broken out by document type and field.

distractors.B: High accuracy is not meaningless; the issue is stratification, not that the number crosses a threshold. Confidence intervals narrow with sample size and are not 'always too wide.'
distractors.C: Recomputing after every extraction confuses ongoing monitoring cadence with the real problem, which is that the aggregate hides per-segment weakness.
distractors.D: 10,000 documents is ample overall; the problem is that the rare segment is under-represented within it, not that the total sample is too small.

scenario: After launch, high-confidence extractions are auto-approved without review. You have budget to hand-check about 2% of these auto-approved outputs per week to measure the true error rate and catch new failure modes, but auto-approved volume is skewed heavily toward two common form types.
stem: How should you select the weekly sample of high-confidence extractions to audit?

options.text: Take a simple random 2% sample across all auto-approved extractions.
Use stratified random sampling across document types and field categories so every segment, including rare ones, contributes enough audited cases to estimate its own error rate.
Audit only the extractions with the very highest confidence scores, since those are most likely to be representative.
Let reviewers pick whichever auto-approved documents look most suspicious to them each week.

rationale.correct: Stratified random sampling guarantees coverage of every document type and field segment, so low-volume strata get enough audited cases to produce a meaningful per-segment error rate and to surface novel error patterns that a volume-weighted sample would miss.

distractors.A: A simple random sample is dominated by the two common form types, so rare segments may get zero or near-zero audited cases and their error rate stays unknown, which is exactly the masking problem.
distractors.C: Sampling only the highest-confidence cases is a biased, non-random slice that tells you nothing about the rest of the high-confidence population and cannot detect emerging failures.
distractors.D: Reviewer-selected 'suspicious' documents is convenience sampling, not random; it inflates the apparent error rate and misses silent failures the model is confidently wrong about.

scenario: Your extraction model emits a confidence score between 0 and 1 for each field. The team wants to auto-approve any field where confidence is at least 0.90, reasoning that 0.90 'obviously means 90% correct.' No one has checked what those scores correspond to in practice.
stem: What must you do before trusting a 0.90 threshold to gate auto-approval?

options.text: Nothing further; a model-reported 0.90 confidence is by definition a 90% probability of being correct.
Raise the threshold to 0.99 for every field so the scores are guaranteed to be conservative.
Calibrate the confidence scores against a labeled validation set to learn what actual accuracy each score band delivers per field, then set the threshold from that evidence.
Average each field's confidence scores into one document-level score and threshold on that instead.

rationale.correct: Raw model confidence is not inherently calibrated; a reported 0.90 may correspond to 99% or 70% real accuracy, and that mapping differs by field. Comparing scores to ground truth on a labeled validation set tells you the true accuracy of each score band so you can set an evidence-based, per-field threshold.

distractors.A: This is the core calibration fallacy: a confidence score is not automatically a probability of correctness until it has been validated against labeled data.
distractors.B: Blindly raising the threshold sends far more fields to review without knowing whether 0.99 is well-calibrated either; it trades cost for a still-unverified assumption.
distractors.D: Averaging field scores into a document score destroys the field-level granularity you need to route review attention to the specific weak fields.

scenario: Reviewer capacity is limited, so you cannot send every extraction to a human. Some source documents are clean with the model highly confident, while others are contradictory (two different totals printed on the same page) or blurry scans where the model's confidence is low.
stem: Which routing policy makes the best use of scarce reviewer capacity?

options.text: Route a fixed random 20% of all extractions to review regardless of confidence or document quality.
Route the oldest documents in the queue to review first, independent of confidence.
Route only documents from the single highest-volume document type, since that is where most errors occur in absolute count.
Route extractions with low model confidence or ambiguous/contradictory source documents to human review, and auto-approve the well-calibrated high-confidence rest.

rationale.correct: Prioritizing low-confidence and ambiguous/contradictory-source extractions concentrates limited reviewer attention where the model is most likely wrong or the source itself is unreliable, while safely auto-approving the calibrated high-confidence remainder.

distractors.A: A fixed random slice ignores the confidence signal entirely, so it wastes reviewer time on easy high-confidence cases while letting many risky low-confidence ones through.
distractors.B: Age of the document has no relationship to error likelihood; ordering by queue time misallocates reviewers away from risky extractions.
distractors.C: Volume is not risk: the highest-volume type may be the most accurate, and this policy ignores confidence and source ambiguity entirely.

scenario: Six weeks after going live, a vendor changes its invoice template. The model keeps extracting the 'total due' field with high confidence, but it is now silently grabbing the subtotal instead. Overall audited accuracy has barely moved because the new template is still rare.
stem: What ongoing practice is most likely to catch this kind of newly introduced, high-confidence error?

options.text: Continuous stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions, with results tracked per document-type and field segment over time to surface emerging error patterns.
Relying on the model's own confidence scores to flag the regression, since a real error will lower its confidence.
Re-reading the one-time pre-launch aggregate accuracy report whenever a problem is suspected.
Waiting for end users to file complaints about wrong totals before investigating.

rationale.correct: Ongoing stratified sampling audits a slice of even the high-confidence, low-volume segments, and tracking error rates per segment over time reveals a drift in one template's 'total due' field that an aggregate number would dilute away.

distractors.B: The failure mode here is precisely a high-confidence error: the model is confidently wrong, so its own score will not flag the regression.
distractors.C: A static pre-launch report reflects the old template distribution and cannot reveal a change that happened weeks after launch.
distractors.D: Waiting for complaints is reactive, slow, and misses errors users never notice; the point of sampling is to detect problems before they cause harm.

scenario: You are preparing a go/no-go decision to reduce human review on a document pipeline. Your validation results show 98% accuracy on typed PDFs and on the 'invoice number' field, but you have not yet broken results out for handwritten forms or for the 'tax ID' field.
stem: What should you require before reducing human review for the whole pipeline?

options.text: Proceed to reduce review everywhere, since 98% on the segments you measured exceeds the target threshold.
Verify accuracy is consistently strong across every document type and every field segment, and keep human review on any segment that has not been validated or underperforms.
Reduce review only for typed PDFs and delete the handwritten and tax-ID segments from the pipeline so they no longer affect metrics.
Combine all segments into one accuracy number; if that combined number is above target, reduce review across the board.

rationale.correct: Automating high-confidence extractions is only safe once accuracy has been validated by document type and field and shown to be consistent across all segments; segments that are unvalidated or weak must keep human review rather than inherit the strong segments' numbers.

distractors.A: Strong results on two measured segments say nothing about handwritten forms or the tax-ID field; extending the decision to unmeasured segments is exactly the masking risk.
distractors.C: Deleting inconvenient segments does not make their documents disappear from the real workload; it just hides the risk instead of validating it.
distractors.D: Re-aggregating into one number reintroduces the dilution problem; the go/no-go must be made segment by segment.

scenario: A colleague drafts the review-calibration plan and asks you to confirm which statement is actually correct before it ships.
stem: Which statement about accuracy metrics and confidence calibration is correct?

options.text: A high aggregate accuracy proves the model performs uniformly, so per-segment validation is redundant once the overall number clears the target.
Model-reported confidence scores are inherently calibrated probabilities, so no labeled validation is needed to set thresholds.

Aggregate accuracy can hide poor performance on specific document types and fields, so you validate per segment, calibrate field-level confidence against a labeled validation set, and use stratified sampling to measure ongoing error rates and detect novel patterns.
Because reviewer capacity is limited, the safest policy is to route a purely random slice of extractions to review rather than prioritizing low-confidence or contradictory-source cases.

rationale.correct: This captures the whole discipline: aggregates mask segment-level weakness, so you validate by document type and field, calibrate field-level confidence against labeled data before trusting thresholds, and use stratified sampling to keep measuring error rates and to catch new failure modes.

distractors.A: A high aggregate does not imply uniform performance; a volume-weighted average can hide a badly failing rare segment, which is why per-segment validation is essential.
distractors.B: Raw confidence scores are not automatically calibrated; you must compare them to ground truth on a labeled validation set before treating them as probabilities of correctness.
distractors.D: Random routing wastes scarce reviewer capacity on easy cases; prioritizing low-confidence and ambiguous/contradictory extractions is the better use of limited human attention.

scenario: You must design an end-to-end plan to safely reduce human review on a mixed-document extraction pipeline while (1) proving performance is acceptable on every segment, (2) deciding which extractions to auto-approve, and (3) continuing to catch new failures after launch, all under a fixed reviewer budget.
stem: Which combination of measures satisfies all three goals?

options.text: Validate accuracy per document type and field before automating; calibrate field-level confidence scores against a labeled validation set to set auto-approval thresholds and route low-confidence or contradictory-source cases to review; and run continuous stratified random sampling of auto-approved outputs, tracked per segment, to measure error rates and detect novel patterns.

Ship once the single aggregate accuracy clears the target; auto-approve everything above a fixed 0.90 raw confidence without validating that score; and re-check the original aggregate report only if someone complains.
Skip per-segment validation to save time; route a fixed random 20% of extractions to review regardless of confidence; and rely on falling model confidence to reveal any regression.
Auto-approve only the highest-volume document type; average field confidences into one document score for thresholding; and audit only the extractions reviewers find suspicious each week.

rationale.correct: Each goal maps to a specific mechanism: per-segment validation proves acceptable performance everywhere, labeled-set calibration plus confidence/ambiguity-based routing decides what to auto-approve within budget, and ongoing stratified sampling tracked per segment keeps measuring error rates and catching novel failures after launch.

distractors.B: A single aggregate hides weak segments, a raw 0.90 score is uncalibrated, and re-reading a static report only on complaint is reactive, so none of the three goals are met.
distractors.C: Skipping per-segment validation leaves the masking risk in place, random routing ignores the confidence signal, and confident-but-wrong errors will not lower the model's confidence, so regressions go undetected.
distractors.D: Volume-based auto-approval ignores per-segment risk, averaging confidences destroys field-level routing granularity, and reviewer-picked 'suspicious' audits are biased convenience samples, not stratified random ones.

scenario: In your multi-agent research system, search subagents return well-cited findings, but by the time the synthesis agent produces the final report, the reader cannot tell which source supports which claim. Each search subagent currently returns a free-text paragraph summarizing what it found.
stem: What change most directly prevents source attribution from being lost through the pipeline?

options.text: Instruct the synthesis agent to append a single 'Sources' section at the end of the report listing every URL any subagent visited.

Require each search subagent to emit structured claim-source mappings (each claim paired with its source URL/document name and a relevant excerpt) that downstream agents preserve and merge through synthesis.
Increase the synthesis agent's max output tokens so it has room to restate the subagents' paragraphs verbatim.
Add a post-hoc citation agent that re-reads the finished report and guesses which of the collected sources most likely supports each sentence.

rationale.correct: Attribution is lost during summarization when findings are compressed as free text without preserving which source backs which claim. Emitting structured claim-source mappings at the subagent level (claim + source URL/document + excerpt) gives the synthesis agent explicit units to carry through and merge, so every claim in the final report remains traceable to its origin.

distractors.A: A bulk 'Sources' list proves the sources were seen but not which claim each one supports; the claim-to-source mapping is exactly what is lost, so a flat list does not restore traceability.
distractors.C: More tokens do not create structure. Restating free-text paragraphs still lacks explicit claim-source pairs, and the attribution decays again at the merge step.
distractors.D: Reconstructing attribution by guessing after the fact is unreliable and can misattribute claims to the wrong source; provenance must be preserved forward, not inferred backward.

scenario: Two credible analyst firms report different figures for the same market's size: Source X says $4.2B and Source Y says $5.1B, both for the current year. Your synthesis agent must produce a single report section on market size.
stem: How should the synthesis agent handle the conflicting statistics?

options.text: Present both figures side by side, annotated with their sources and any methodological notes, and flag the discrepancy rather than resolving it silently.
Average the two figures to $4.65B and report the single blended value as the market size.
Report only the higher figure from Source Y, since a larger addressable market is the more useful planning assumption.
Report only the figure from whichever source appears first in the subagents' combined output to keep the section concise.

rationale.correct: When credible sources conflict, the correct behavior is to annotate the conflict with source attribution (and methodological context) rather than arbitrarily selecting one value. Surfacing both figures with their provenance lets the reader or coordinator judge the discrepancy instead of hiding it behind a false single answer.

distractors.B: Averaging manufactures a number that neither source reported and erases the fact that credible sources disagree; it fabricates false precision.
distractors.C: Choosing the higher value 'because it's more useful' is arbitrary selection biased by a planning preference, not a source- or methodology-grounded decision, and it suppresses a real conflict.
distractors.D: Ordering in the combined output is an accident of aggregation, not evidence of correctness; picking by position is arbitrary selection.

scenario: A research subagent returns two unemployment statistics for the same country that appear to contradict each other: 3.8% and 4.3%. On inspection, one was published in a Q1 report and the other in a Q3 report, but neither figure carried a date in the subagent's output.
stem: What is the most effective way to prevent this class of false contradiction going forward?

options.text: Instruct the synthesis agent to keep only the most recent-sounding figure whenever two statistics differ.
Lower the subagents' temperature so they extract statistics more deterministically.
Require every subagent to include the publication or data-collection date alongside each statistic in its structured output.
Have the coordinator discard any topic where two subagents return differing numbers to avoid reporting contradictions.

rationale.correct: The two figures are not contradictory; they describe different time periods. Requiring publication/collection dates in structured outputs lets downstream agents interpret temporal differences correctly instead of misreading them as conflicts. Dates are the metadata that disambiguates time-varying data.

distractors.A: 'Most recent-sounding' is a guess; without recorded dates the agent cannot reliably tell which figure is newer, and silently dropping one hides valid temporal data.
distractors.B: Temperature affects generation variability, not whether time metadata is captured; the numbers were both correct for their periods, so determinism does not address the root cause.
distractors.D: Discarding the topic throws away valid information; the figures only look contradictory because dates were missing, which is fixable by capturing the dates.

scenario: Your synthesis agent assembles a report combining quarterly revenue figures, breaking industry news, and an API migration checklist. To keep formatting 'consistent,' it currently converts everything into flowing prose paragraphs.
stem: What rendering approach best serves the reader across these content types?

options.text: Keep everything as uniform prose so the report has one consistent voice and is easy to read top to bottom.
Render each content type in its most legible form: financial data as tables, news as prose, and the migration checklist as a structured list.
Convert everything into a single large table, since tables are the most information-dense format.
Render everything as a bulleted list so each fact is individually scannable regardless of its type.

rationale.correct: Synthesis outputs should render different content types appropriately rather than forcing a uniform format: financial/numeric data belongs in tables where values align and compare, narrative news reads best as prose, and sequential technical steps are clearest as structured lists. Matching form to content preserves meaning and usability.

distractors.A: Flattening tabular revenue figures and step-by-step procedures into prose destroys the comparability and sequence that those content types depend on.
distractors.C: A single giant table forces narrative news into a grid it does not fit and obscures rather than clarifies non-tabular content.
distractors.D: Uniform bullets strip the columnar structure numbers need and the narrative flow news needs; 'one format for everything' is the anti-pattern here.

scenario: Three subagents each return structured claim-source mappings. Two of them independently support the claim 'adoption grew year over year' but cite different sources; a third reports a distinct claim about pricing. The synthesis agent must merge these into one report.
stem: How should the synthesis agent merge the structured mappings?

options.text: Deduplicate by keeping only one subagent's mapping per topic and dropping the others to avoid repetition.
Collapse all three mappings into a single citation pointing to whichever source is most authoritative overall.
Merge the mappings while preserving each claim's full set of supporting sources, so the corroborated adoption claim retains both citations and the pricing claim retains its own.
Concatenate the raw mapping objects into an appendix and write the report body as unattributed prose.

rationale.correct: Merging must preserve the claim-source structure: a claim corroborated by two sources should carry both citations (which strengthens it), and distinct claims keep their own sources. Preserving and merging structured mappings is precisely what keeps provenance intact through synthesis.

distractors.A: Dropping subagents' mappings discards corroborating evidence; two independent sources supporting one claim is valuable signal, not redundant noise to prune.
distractors.B: Collapsing to a single 'most authoritative' citation throws away the corroboration and the other source's attribution, weakening traceability.
distractors.D: Writing the body as unattributed prose reintroduces exactly the attribution loss the structured mappings exist to prevent; an appendix does not tie claims to sources.

scenario: A document-analysis subagent finds two conflicting compliance-cost figures within the same set of filings. It is tempted to pick the value it judges more reliable before handing results to the coordinator.
stem: What should the document-analysis subagent do with the conflicting values?

options.text: Silently select the value it judges more reliable and pass only that one forward to keep the handoff clean.
Include both conflicting values with explicit annotation and source attribution, and let the coordinator decide how to reconcile before synthesis.
Drop both values and note only that 'a conflict exists' without the numbers, to avoid propagating an error.
Escalate to a human immediately and halt its analysis until the conflict is resolved.

rationale.correct: Analysis subagents should complete their work with conflicting values included and explicitly annotated, leaving reconciliation to the coordinator, which has the broader cross-source view. Resolving conflicts too early, inside an isolated subagent, discards context the coordinator needs to make the right call.

distractors.A: A subagent resolving the conflict silently is arbitrary selection made without the coordinator's full context, and it hides the disagreement downstream agents need to see.
distractors.C: Dropping the numbers destroys the very data needed to reconcile; annotating a conflict requires keeping the conflicting values and their sources.
distractors.D: Halting on every intra-document conflict is disproportionate; the standard flow is to annotate and continue, letting the coordinator reconcile, not to block the pipeline.

scenario: A synthesis report warns readers of a 'contradiction' between two credible cybersecurity studies: one states breach costs rose and another states they fell. The underlying data was collected in different years, but the report presented both as current, undated claims.
stem: What is the primary root cause of the spurious contradiction, and the fix?

options.text: The sources are not actually credible; the fix is to filter out one of them during retrieval.
The synthesis model hallucinated; the fix is a stronger system prompt telling it not to invent contradictions.

Temporal metadata was dropped, so time-separated data points were compared as if simultaneous; the fix is carrying collection/publication dates through to the output so the trend is read across time, not as a conflict.
The report format is too long; the fix is to summarize both studies into a single sentence.

rationale.correct: The 'contradiction' is an artifact of missing temporal context: two measurements from different periods were treated as simultaneous. Preserving collection/publication dates through to the structured output lets the synthesis correctly present the figures as a trend over time rather than a conflict.

distractors.A: Both sources are credible and both figures may be correct for their years; filtering a good source suppresses valid data and does not address the missing-date root cause.
distractors.B: The model did not fabricate the numbers; it faithfully compared real figures that lacked dates. A prompt telling it not to 'invent contradictions' ignores the actual absence of temporal metadata.
distractors.D: Shortening the text does not supply the missing dates; compression would more likely worsen attribution and temporal loss.

scenario: You are writing the output specification for a synthesis agent that produces investor briefings combining well-established findings, hotly contested projections, financial statements, and market commentary.
stem: Which output specification best preserves provenance and communicates uncertainty?

options.text: Separate sections for well-established versus contested findings, preserving each source's original characterization and methodological context; financials rendered as tables and commentary as prose; every claim carrying its source attribution.
One confidence score per paragraph averaged across all claims, with sources omitted to keep the briefing uncluttered.
A single ranked list of conclusions ordered by the synthesis agent's confidence, with contested and established findings interleaved and sources footnoted only where convenient.
All content normalized into identical prose blocks with a shared bibliography, so established and contested claims read the same for consistency.

rationale.correct: A robust spec distinguishes well-established findings from contested ones (preserving original source characterizations and methodological context), renders each content type appropriately (financials as tables, commentary as prose), and keeps per-claim source attribution. This preserves provenance and makes uncertainty explicit.

distractors.B: A single averaged confidence per paragraph blurs which specific claims are contested and, by omitting sources, discards provenance entirely.
distractors.C: Interleaving contested and established findings and footnoting sources only 'where convenient' erases the established-versus-contested distinction and leaves attribution incomplete.
distractors.D: Normalizing everything into identical prose flattens content types and makes contested claims indistinguishable from established ones, hiding uncertainty for the sake of superficial consistency.
